definition: A ledger that records activity in batches called blocks. Each block includes a cryptographic reference to its predecessor, allowing participants to check the history.
The output of a function that turns input data into a fixed-size value. A cryptographic hash helps check data integrity; it does not conceal the input.
A cryptographic value that can be shared so others can verify a digital signature. It is paired mathematically with a private key.
A secret value used to produce digital signatures. In a crypto account, these signatures can authorise spending, so losing control of the key can mean losing control of assets.
A tool for interacting with blockchain accounts. Some wallets manage signing keys and submit transactions; watch-only wallets display activity without being able to spend.
Responsibility for controlling and safeguarding assets. With self-custody, the holder manages signing access; with a custodial service, a provider manages it for the customer.

The method a network uses to select the transaction history its participants accept when different histories are proposed. Consensus operates alongside rules that determine whether transactions are valid.
A mechanism that requires miners to find a computational solution before proposing a block. Other nodes can check that solution and reject blocks that break network rules.
A mechanism that uses validators with committed crypto assets to propose or approve blocks. Network rules determine participation, rewards and penalties.
The status or level of confidence indicating that a recorded blockchain result will remain accepted. Some systems build confidence over additional blocks; others use explicit validator agreement.
Code deployed on a blockchain that participants execute according to agreed rules. It can manage assets or application state, but can also contain bugs or dangerous permissions.
A crypto asset intended to maintain a price linked to something else, commonly one unit of a national currency. Maintaining that price depends on its design and is not guaranteed.
A measure of the work required to execute operations on Ethereum and some other networks. The amount of gas used and its price contribute to the fee paid for a transaction.
The name of a blockchain network that uses proof of work to maintain a payment ledger. Its native asset is bitcoin, commonly identified by the symbol BTC.
A blockchain network that runs applications through smart contracts. Ether, identified by ETH, is its native asset and is used to pay for network operations.
A digital asset whose transfers are authorised using cryptography and recorded according to the rules of its network.
The native crypto asset of a blockchain, such as bitcoin on Bitcoin or ether on Ethereum.
An asset represented under an existing blockchain's token rules or smart contracts. Its rights and risks depend on its design and issuer.
A broad term for a cryptocurrency other than bitcoin. It does not imply a particular technology, purpose or level of safety.
A sequence of words used by compatible wallets to recover cryptographic keys. Anyone obtaining it may be able to control the associated assets.
A venue or service for trading assets. It may use a central operator, on-chain smart contracts, or a combination of systems.
An estimate calculated by multiplying an asset's current price by its circulating supply. It is not the cash held by the market or available for withdrawal.
The degree to which a market price changes over a period. Higher volatility means larger price movements, without predicting their direction.
How readily an asset can be bought or sold without substantially changing its price. Liquidity depends on the venue, order size and market conditions.
A request to change a ledger's state, such as transferring an asset. A valid request must meet the network's authorisation and execution rules.
